system_prompt:
You are distilling one chapter of a guitar method book into a short summary.

The user will give you a chapter file with topic-organized verbatim quotes
plus the human-rationale notes for each. Write a one-paragraph summary (4-7
sentences) that captures:

  - what this chapter teaches (the techniques, concepts, rules, examples)
  - the master's characteristic moves visible in this chapter (if any)
  - the load-bearing terminology this chapter introduces

Reference the topic labels from the chapter file when useful. Do not invent
information not present in the chapter. If the chapter is biographical or
introductory rather than instructional, say so explicitly.

Output just the paragraph — no preamble, no JSON, no markdown formatting.

# Chapter 13 — Professional Fingerstyle Jazz Guitar, Part 2: Self accompanying

_Pages 121-130._

> **Verbatim-quote constraint.** The quotes below are exact substrings of the raw transcript produced by `pdftotext`. The transcript may contain extraction artifacts where the book's typeface confuses the tool — e.g. `7irst` or `<irst` for `first`, `speci7ic` for `specific`. **Do NOT manually fix these in this file**: the quote-fidelity validator compares against the raw transcript, so a 'fixed' quote will fail verification and break Stage 2 idempotency. If a future pipeline iteration adds artifact-normalization, it must normalize the transcript and these files together.

## Mixed harmonic movement

> It is most common to find mixed harmonic movement. This example starts on a | chord and
> moves to a V chord which sets it up for a cycle move to Cmaj7 in the second measure. Notice that
> the lowest note of Gmaj7 in the first measure is D, the fifth, and the lowest note of G7(5) is b5.
> This was done to continue the effect of chromatic movement from Gmaj7 to G7(5) to Cmaj7. The
> harmony then moves by half step to the finish.

**Significance (p. 120).** Demonstrates how diatonic, chromatic, and cycle-of-fifths movements combine in real progressions.

## Diminished as passing chord

> In many cases the diminished seventh chord is the in-between, the hamburger helper of

**Significance (p. 121).** Names the diminished seventh chord as the standard connector for ascending chromatic harmonic movement.

## Self accompaniment overview

> These self accompaniment techniques start very simply and move quickly to more sophisticated
> ways and means. As a group they include an accelerated condensation of the entire second section
> of this book, Creating Fingerstyle Jazz Guitar Solos, plus more advanced techniques.
>
> The top notes of the first several examples are just simple place holders. This way you can easily
> concentrate on the self accompanying devices.

**Significance (p. 121).** Frames Section Three Part 2 as an accelerated recap of Section Two plus advanced techniques, with simple melody placeholders.

## Doubled bass notes style

> These measures have doubled bass notes, a style used by musicians playing upright bass in the
> swing era of jazz. Otherwise, the movement of harmony is the same as the first example above.

**Significance (p. 122).** Introduces the swing-era doubled-bass-note technique as a specific self-accompaniment device.

## Root/fifth alternation in jazz

> In this self accompanying style the bass alternates between the root and the fifth of each chord.
> Root/fifth is often associated with simple music, such as polka bands, country music and the like.
> Root/fifth is used in jazz too, but usually not in such a rigid oom-pah fashion.

**Significance (p. 123).** Defines root/fifth alternation and distinguishes the jazz use from simpler genres.

## Root/seventh alternation

> This chord progression moves in an upward direction. !t is another example of an alternating
> pattern from low root note to upper note. However, in this case the upper note is a major, minor, or
> diminished seventh interval except for the last interval, which begins on the third of the Ft 7 chord
> and moves to its root. Keeping a strict pattern of root/seventh is not as important as long as the effect
> (low to high alternation) is there.

**Significance (p. 124).** Introduces root/seventh alternation as the more sophisticated sibling of root/fifth, with the rule that the alternating effect matters more than strict interval choice.

## Walking bass technique

> This accompaniment device emulates jazz bass by using scale step notes in-between chord
> tones. It’s very smooth sounding. The root of each chord is still evident.

**Significance (p. 125).** Defines the walking bass technique for guitar: scale-step passing tones between chord tones with the root still audible.

> chord root notes — by half step.

**Significance (p. 126).** States the chromatic approach-note rule: chord roots are commonly approached from a half step below.

## Leading with bass note

> Leading with a bass note is a way to give variety to accompaniment instead of just chugging
> along with four bass notes to a measure.

**Significance (p. 126).** Introduces the bass-lead device as a rhythmic variation to avoid monotonous quarter-note bass patterns.

## Two-note accompaniment sufficiency

> A melody accompanied by two additional notes is often all you need to make an arrangement
> sound full, whether you are playing by yourself or with a group.

**Significance (p. 127).** States the economy principle: two accompanying notes can create a full-sounding arrangement.

## Swing-era tenths accompaniment

> Moving tenths in the left hand was one of the primary accompanying devices of pianists in the
> swing era. Fats Waller, Willie “The Lion” Smith, Art Tatum, Teddy Wilson, and many others made
> this the style until bebop came along. Within reason, you can emulate it on the guitar. The pianists
> mentioned often kept almost constant quarter-note moving tenths going with the melody. You
> should be able to manage at least half notes. Go for it.

**Significance (p. 128).** Links guitar tenths technique to the swing-era piano tradition of Waller, Tatum, and Wilson, setting a half-note minimum for guitar.

## II-V-I movement pattern

> The most common harmonic movement in jazz is II-V-l. It is often repeated through a portion of
> the cycle of fifths. A smooth way to incorporate this into your playing is to use the pattern shown
> below: a minor seventh defined by a root and seventh followed by the dominant seventh defined with
> just root and third. They both point to the | chord, third measure, which is both the end of a cadence
> and the beginning of the next movement. The bass is still using root movement.

**Significance (p. 129).** Names II-V-I as the most common jazz harmonic movement and gives a specific voicing recipe using root+seventh then root+third.

## Fourths and tritones voicing

> This variation uses the same chords except the accompaniment is voiced so that the harmony
> moves in alternating pairs of fourths and tritones. The bottom note in each pair alternates between
> major or minor seventh to major third. There is no explicitly stated root or fifth of the chord. If you play
> in a group, the bassist will cover roots and fifths.

**Significance (p. 130).** Introduces fourths/tritones voicing as an alternative to root-position voicing, with the rule that a bassist covers the omitted roots.
